about: Physics blocks whose maths is a formula (ND3b): each keeps its id, ports and results, and its maths is the Equation below, with a name that says what happens.

references: Stefan-Boltzmann law; definition of effective temperature, e.g. Carroll, B. W. and Ostlie, D. A. 2017, An Introduction to Modern Astrophysics, 2nd edn, Cambridge University Press, eq. 3.17. doi:10.1017/9781108380980

equation.name: How hot a star's surface shines

source.text: Carroll, B. W. and Ostlie, D. A. 2017, An Introduction to Modern Astrophysics, 2nd edn, Cambridge University Press

explain.curious: How hot a star's surface is follows from how much light leaves how much surface.
explain.science: Effective temperature is the temperature of a black body with the star's radius and luminosity. It defines the surface temperature rather than measuring it.

references: Hansen, C. J., Kawaler, S. D. and Trimble, V. 2004, Stellar Interiors, 2nd edn, Springer, section 1.4 (main-sequence lifetime scaling). doi:10.1007/978-1-4419-9110-2

equation.name: How long a star burns hydrogen

source.text: Hansen, C. J., Kawaler, S. D. and Trimble, V. 2004, Stellar Interiors, 2nd edn, Springer

explain.curious: A star lives on its fuel divided by how fast it burns it. Bright heavy stars burn out in millions of years; dim red dwarfs outlast the present age of the universe.
explain.science: The usable hydrogen scales with mass and the burn rate with luminosity, so the lifetime scales as M/L, normalised to the Sun's 10 Gyr. Ignores the larger burnt fraction in fully convective dwarfs and mass loss in massive stars.

params.description: share of the envelope's binding energy the star must radiate (0.5, matching the 1.5e7 yr of Hurley, Tout and Pols 2002 eq. 61)

references: Hurley, J. R., Tout, C. A. and Pols, O. R. 2002, Evolution of binary stars and the effect of tides on binary populations, MNRAS 329, 897: overflow rate F(M) [ln(R/R_L)]³ M☉/yr with F = 3e-6 (min(M, 5))² (eq. 58), capped by the donor's thermal timescale τ_KH = 1.5e7 M (M − M_c) / (R L) yr in solar units (eq. 61). https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0201220
Kelvin, Lord 1862 and Helmholtz, H. von 1856: a star's thermal timescale is the time its light takes to carry off its gravitational binding energy.
atoms.shown: τ_KH = k G M (M − M_c) / (R L)

equation.name: How long a star takes to settle after its outer layers are disturbed
equation.formula: tau = k * G * M * max(M - Mc, 0) / (R * L)

tau.name: time for the star's light to carry off its envelope's binding energy

source.text: Hurley, J. R., Tout, C. A. and Pols, O. R. 2002, MNRAS 329, 897

explain.curious: A star can only shrink or swell as fast as its light carries energy away: for the Sun about thirty million years, for a giant's loose envelope a few thousand.
explain.science: The Kelvin-Helmholtz time of the envelope. It caps how fast a star can hand gas to a partner, and how fast a partner can take it. Unverified until the paper search returns.

references: Hurley, J. R., Tout, C. A. and Pols, O. R. 2002, MNRAS 329, 897, eq. 50: magnetic braking J̇ = −5.83e-16 (M_env/M) (R ω)³ M☉ R☉² yr⁻² (R in R☉, ω in yr⁻¹), after Rappaport, Verbunt and Joss 1983, ApJ 275, 713. https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0201220

equation.name: How fast a star's magnetised wind brakes its spin
equation.formula:
rw = R / R_sun * w * yr
jdot = -k * (Me / M) * rw * rw * rw * M_sun * R_sun * R_sun / (yr * yr)

w.name: how fast it turns, radians a second

jdot.name: spin angular momentum carried off each second (negative)

source.text: Hurley, J. R., Tout, C. A. and Pols, O. R. 2002, MNRAS 329, 897

explain.curious: A star with a churning outer layer flings its wind out along its magnetic field, like a skater flinging out arms, and slows down.
explain.science: The Skumanich-type braking law used by the binary code BSE. In a close pair the tides lock the star's spin to the orbit, so the brake drains the orbit itself and the stars draw together: how cataclysmic variables above the period gap are fed. Unverified until the paper search returns.
